# Levi Foster — iPhone Apps, Photography Tools and Generative Art
Source: https://lf.wtf/

### Projects

## Levi Foster
Independent app developer and artist · Fort Worth, Texas
I am Levi Foster. I build iPhone apps and make things with code, mostly at the point where photography stops being a picture and starts being a process. Some of it ships on the App Store. The rest ends up as prints.
The apps share a bias. I would rather simulate the thing than approximate the look of it, which is slower and more awkward and gets results a preset cannot. That is the whole idea behind FRMT, and it is why MODUL8 models broken hardware instead of drawing coloured lines over your photo.

### Work

### FRMT — Film Simulation
A film simulation camera for iPhone. It models the photographic process itself rather than applying a colour filter: light scattering through the emulsion, dye layers holding each other back, grain forming where the light actually landed. Four stocks, built from published manufacturer measurements, developed from a RAW negative on the device.

### MODUL8 — Glitch Art Effects
A glitch art app for iPhone. Nineteen stackable effects, each modelled on a specific way real hardware used to fail: VHS tracking loss, CRT phosphor bloom, datamosh block corruption, pixel sorting, channel separation. Reorder the layers and the picture changes.

### Harmony Palette
A colour harmony and design tool for iPhone and iPad.

### Merge With The Machine
An art project about the line where human imagination meets machine generation. Generated visuals, experimental tools, and a print shop.

### Elsewhere
- App Store
- Instagram
- X
- TikTok
- Etsy
- GitHub

### Contact
Email L@LF.WTF. That reaches me directly.

# FRMT — Film Simulation App for iPhone
Source: https://lf.wtf/frmt/

## FRMT
Film Simulation for iPhone

### Not a filter. A film.
Every other film app on your phone is a colour filter. A list of what each colour should become, applied to a photo that has already been taken.
FRMT simulates the film instead. The light scattering sideways through the emulsion. The dye layers chemically holding each other back. The grain forming only where light actually landed. Your iPhone runs the chemistry, one frame at a time, from a RAW negative.
No subscription · No account · Nothing leaves your phone
The difference

### A filter is a list. Film is a reaction.
A filter works by lookup. Somebody decided in advance what every colour should turn into, and the app swaps them one pixel at a time. Feed it the same blue twice and you get the same answer twice, whether that blue was an inch of evening sky or the highlight on a chrome bumper.
Film has no list to consult. It has chemistry, and chemistry pays attention to its surroundings. Light that hits a bright edge keeps going, bounces off the back of the film and comes back to expose the grains beside it. Dye forming in one layer releases a chemical that stops the layer next to it forming as strongly. Grain appears where enough photons happened to land, which is not the same place in the shadows as in the midtones.
None of that can be written down as a list, because the answer depends on what else is in the frame.
That is the whole reason a neon sign on film glows into the dark around it, why reds stay separate from greens instead of turning to mud, and why grain sits heaviest in the midtones and vanishes in deep shadow. It is what people are pointing at when they say a photograph looks like film. A lookup table cannot get there, no matter how carefully it was made.
The proof

### We built the filter, then beat it.
One photograph, developed twice. On the left, the best possible colour filter of this exact film stock, built from the same measurements we built the model from. On the right, the full simulation. This is a 1:1 crop, so you are looking at real pixels rather than a resized version of them.
Zoom back out and it is everywhere. Here is every place the two versions disagree across the whole frame, amplified and shown on its own. This is the light a filter cannot produce, because producing it means moving light across the frame rather than recolouring it in place.
Three things a filter cannot do

### What your phone is actually calculating.
Every photograph goes through these in order, the same order a negative goes through them, on the graphics processor in your phone.
Halation, on its own

### This is real, and it is in every frame.
The returning light from a single photograph, pulled out and amplified so you can see it. Nothing here was painted on. It is what the model produced from the negative.
Four stocks

### Measured, not styled.
The numbers behind each one come off its manufacturer's own published datasheet: the response curves, the spectral sensitivity, the grain figures. Nobody sat down and eyeballed a preset until it looked about right.
You load one at a time, the way you load a roll. There is no look picker on the capture screen and there are no sliders, and none of the four is a variation on another.
How it works

### A camera, not a control panel.
- Press the shutter. A RAW negative is written immediately. The shutter never waits on processing, so the app stays as fast as the stock camera.
- It goes on the roll. Frames queue up exactly like exposures on a roll of film. Keep shooting. You can also set developing to hold until you are plugged in.
- It develops. About a minute a frame, on your phone, running the full model from negative to print. You watch the timer, not a progress bar pretending to be one.
- You get it back. Finished photographs save to your photo library and stay in the app, so you can look through them without leaving. Shot something on another camera? Import the RAW and develop that too.
Honestly

### It is slow, and that is the trade.
A minute of your phone's graphics processor per photograph is an absurd amount of computation to spend on one image, and it is the reason nobody else does this. A filter is one lookup per pixel and it is done before you lift your thumb. We think the minute buys something a lookup never will.
The viewfinder shows you the scene, not the film. Grading a live preview means guessing at the answer before the work is done, and a preview that guesses wrong is worse than one that is honest. Use the exposure dial to place your highlights.
This is slide film. There is not much room above the highlights. That is faithful rather than accidental, and it is the part that will change how you shoot.
One price, once

### $14.99. That is the whole business model.
No subscription, no account, no cloud, no ads, no watermark, no in app purchases, no upsell to unlock the good stocks. Your photographs never leave your phone, because the app has no networking code in it at all.
Requires an iPhone that can capture Apple ProRAW.
Questions

### The things people ask first.

**How is FRMT different from a film filter or a LUT?**
A filter is a lookup table. Somebody decided in advance what every colour becomes, and the same input always gives the same output. FRMT simulates the process instead, so what happens to a pixel depends on what surrounds it: light spreads sideways into neighbouring areas, dye layers hold each other back, and grain forms according to how much light actually landed.

**Which film stocks are included?**
Four, each built from its manufacturer's published characteristic curves and spectral sensitivity data rather than eyeballed from somebody's scans.

**Is it a subscription?**
No. One purchase of $14.99. No subscription, no account, no advertising, no in app purchases.

**Do my photos leave my iPhone?**
No. Every frame is developed on the iPhone's own GPU. The app contains no networking code at all, so there is nothing to upload and no server holding a copy.

**Why does developing take so long?**
Because it runs the chemistry rather than looking up an answer. Light transport through the emulsion, the interaction between dye layers and grain formation are all computed for every frame, and that costs real time on a phone.

**Which iPhones does it work on?**
Any iPhone that can capture Apple ProRAW, running iOS 26 or later.
FRMT is built by Levi Foster in Fort Worth, Texas

# MODUL8 — Glitch Art App for iPhone | Free Glitch Photo Effects
Source: https://lf.wtf/modul8/

Glitch art app for iPhone

## Break your photos on purpose.
MODUL8 is an image modulation kit for iPhone. Nineteen effects, each one modelled on a specific way that real hardware used to fail: tape that lost tracking, tubes that bloomed at the edges, compression that gave up halfway through a frame. Stack them, reorder them, and turn a photo into something that looks like it came off a machine that was already dying.
It is free, every effect runs on your phone, and your photos never leave the device.
The idea

### A filter paints over a photo. MODUL8 damages it.
Most glitch apps ship one look. They lay a fixed pattern of coloured lines over whatever you give them, and every photo comes out wearing the same costume. You can spot the app from across a feed.
MODUL8 works the other way round. Each effect is a small simulation of one real failure, and it reads the actual pixels underneath before deciding what to do to them. Pixel Sort finds the bright regions in your specific frame and drags them until the buildings turn to vertical rain. Datamosh picks blocks and pastes them somewhere they do not belong. VHS bleeds colour sideways the way a worn tape head did. Feed two different photos to the same settings and you get two different pictures, because the damage is a response to the image rather than a layer on top of it.
Nothing is baked in. Nineteen effects, any number of them at once, in any order you like.
What is actually in there

### Nineteen effects. Every one of them is a real failure mode.
They are not variations on a theme. Each one models something different, which is why stacking them gets interesting instead of muddy.

### Analogue video
VHS tracking errors, head switching noise at the bottom of the frame, chroma delay, interlacing comb, signal sync loss, analogue static. This is the family that makes a picture look like it was recorded off a television at two in the morning.

### Data corruption
Datamosh copies blocks from one part of the frame into another and smears the motion between them, the way a video file does when the keyframes go missing. Corruption and Pixel Shift tear rows sideways. Pixel Sort reorders pixels by brightness until solid objects run like wet paint.

### Display and colour
CRT adds phosphor glow, barrel curvature and a shadow mask. Bit Crush and Dither drop the colour depth to something a machine from 1994 could hold. RGB Split pulls the three channels apart. Film Grain and Noise put texture back on top.
Same photo, different damage

### The stack decides the picture.
Five renders from two source frames, changed only by which effects were switched on and what order they ran in. Order matters: sorting a photo and then splitting the channels is not the same picture as splitting the channels first and sorting after.
The interface

### One screen. Everything on it does one thing.
The canvas is at the top and it updates while you drag. Underneath it are nine presets to get you somewhere in one tap, then the layer stack showing exactly what is running and in what order, then the effect rack. Tap an effect to open its own parameters. No menus, no modes, no hunting.
Load a photo from your library, or shoot one in the app.
Tap a preset. VHS, CRT, Cyber, Ghost, Retro, Film, Melt, Static or Fried.
Open any effect and move its sliders. Intensity, and then whatever else that particular effect has: block size, tracking, spacing, curvature, threshold.
Drag the layers into a different order and watch the picture change.
Export to your camera roll, or save the whole stack as a preset of your own.
On the device

### Your photos stay on your phone.
Every effect runs locally. There is no upload, no account, no render queue and no server holding a copy of anything you shot. The app is six megabytes and the editing works in aeroplane mode.
It is also why the sliders feel live: you are dragging the real image rather than waiting on a round trip to somebody's GPU. The free version does serve ads, which is the one part that talks to the network. Premium removes them.
Video too

### Loops, not just stills.
Turn any finished image into a seamless looping video with the effect parameters animating across the loop. The tracking drifts, the sort threshold moves, the channels breathe. It exports straight to your camera roll at a size that posts cleanly.
The deal

### Free. Premium is optional.
Every one of the nineteen effects and all nine presets are free, with no limit on how many you stack. Nothing is held hostage behind a paywall and nothing you export is watermarked. Premium is about output and comfort, not about unlocking the tools.
- Free All 19 effects, all 9 presets, unlimited stacking, save and share, no watermark
- Premium Full resolution export, looping video export, saving your own presets, no ads
Questions

### The things people ask first.

### Is MODUL8 free?
Yes. All 19 effects, all 9 presets and unlimited stacking are free, and nothing you export is watermarked. Premium adds full resolution export, looping video export, saving your own presets, and removes ads.

### What effects are in it?
Noise, Pixel Shift, RGB Split, Scanlines, Distortion, Corruption, Feedback, VHS, CRT, Chroma, Film Grain, Bit Crush, Interlace, Invert, Datamosh, Dither, Analogue Static, Pixel Sort and Signal Sync. Any number at once, in any order.

### How is it different from other glitch apps?
Most of them lay a fixed pattern over whatever you give them, so every photo comes out wearing the same costume. Each MODUL8 effect models one specific hardware failure and reads the pixels underneath before deciding what to do, so the same settings give different results on different photographs.

### Does it upload my photos?
No. Every effect runs locally on your iPhone. There is no account, no render queue and no server holding your images. The free version serves ads, which is the only part of the app that touches the network.

### Can it make glitch videos?
Yes. Any finished image can be exported as a seamless looping video with the effect parameters animating across the loop, straight to your camera roll.

### Which iPhones does it work on?
Any iPhone running iOS 15 or later. The app is about 6 MB.

# CYANO: Cyanotype App for iPhone. Real Chemistry, Simulated.
Source: https://lf.wtf/cyano/

## CYANO

Cyanotype Photos

### Not a blue filter.The chemistry.

A cyanotype is the oldest surviving photographic process. Paper brushed with iron salts, a negative laid on top, left out in the sun. What develops is Prussian blue, washed out in plain water. It is where the word blueprint comes from.

CYANO does that chemistry in software. Not a colour swap tuned by eye, but the sensitiser's ultraviolet response integrated against sunlight across the spectrum, and Prussian blue built up through the Beer-Lambert law. No darkroom, no chemicals, no printer.

No subscription · No account · Nothing leaves your phone

Same frame. Drag it.

Why it looks like that

### The paper cannot see most of your photograph.

Cyanotype paper is blind to red and green. It responds only to ultraviolet and the deepest blue, which means it reads a scene at completely the wrong brightness, and that is the whole point of it.

Look at the picture above. To the camera, those yellow flowers and that sky are the same brightness: measure them and the flowers come out at 177, the sky at 167. You could not tell them apart in a black and white conversion.

On the paper they end up at opposite ends. The flowers fall to 57 and the sky rises to 222, because yellow carries almost no light this sensitiser can use while the sky is carrying more than the sheet can hold. Nothing was adjusted to make that happen; it is what the chemistry does.

Two colours your camera recorded as equally bright come out at opposite ends of the print.

A filter cannot get there. A filter is a list somebody wrote down in advance, so it can make a photograph blue, but it has no idea which blue was carrying ultraviolet. That is the difference between something that looks vaguely antique and something that looks like it came out of a tray.

What is actually being computed

### Built from the physics, not from a preset.

Every colour on your screen is three numbers. Those three numbers do not say how much ultraviolet a thing reflected, and ultraviolet is the only part this process cares about. So the model reconstructs the smoothest full spectrum consistent with the colour you photographed, then reads the part of it the sensitiser can actually see.

That spectrum is integrated against the sensitiser's action curve and the solar spectrum to get an exposure. The exposure runs through a tonal curve derived from the photochemistry rather than drawn by hand. The resulting Prussian blue is built up by the Beer-Lambert law, including the way the pigment clumps at high concentration, without which the deep tones stall at an unconvincing electric blue.

It also reads each photograph before printing it, the way a printer reads a negative and makes a test strip, so the exposure suits the picture in front of it rather than some imagined average one.

The controls

### Four dials, and every one of them is real.

**Sun**

How long the sheet was left out. Overexpose it and the shadows merge into one mass, the way they really do.

**Paper**

Cotton rag, rough watercolour, or buff. The base colour shows through everywhere, because in this process the paper is part of the picture.

**Toning**

Tea, tannin or red wine. These convert the Prussian blue into iron tannate rather than tinting it, which is why a toned print reads as another process instead of a recoloured one.

**Brushed edge**

The uneven coating of a hand-brushed sheet, seeded per photograph, so two prints of the same picture are never quite the same.

On your phone

### Simple in front, heavy underneath.

Choose a photograph and it develops. Move the sun, change the paper, drop it in a toning bath. Save at full resolution with nothing stamped on it.

Common questions

### Questions

#### Do I need chemicals, paper or a printer?

None of them. CYANO exists so that people who could never set up a darkroom, buy sensitiser or wait for a sunny afternoon can still make cyanotypes.

#### Is this a filter?

No. A filter decides in advance what each colour becomes. CYANO works out how much ultraviolet each colour was actually carrying and builds the pigment from that.

#### What does it cost?

The app is free and completely usable: unlimited prints, full resolution, no watermark. One optional purchase of $4.99 unlocks the three toning baths, the other two papers and the second sensitiser formula. There is no subscription.

#### Does it collect anything?

No. No account, no analytics, no server, and no networking code of its own. Photographs never leave your phone. The privacy policy is one page and says so.

### Make one.

Free, and the free version is the whole simulation. Nothing is watermarked and nothing is held back to make a point.

# Privacy — FRMT
Source: https://lf.wtf/frmt/privacy/

## Privacy Policy
Last updated: 4 August 2026

### The short version
FRMT does not collect anything about you, and it has no way to. There is no account, no analytics, no advertising and no server. The app contains no networking code at all.

### What the app stores, and where
Everything stays on your iPhone.
Photographs. When you press the shutter, a RAW negative is written to a working folder inside the app. When it finishes developing, the photograph is saved to your photo library and a copy is kept in the app so you can look at it without leaving. The negative is then deleted. You can delete photographs from the app at any time, and deleting one there does not touch the copy in your photo library.
Settings. Which film is loaded, capture size, when developing runs, and whether you have seen the introduction. These live in the app's own preferences and are read by nothing else.
None of this is backed up to iCloud: both folders are marked excluded, because they are a working copy of pictures that are already in your photo library.

### Permissions the app asks for
Camera. To take photographs. Refusing it leaves the rest of the app working, including developing anything already on the roll.
Adding to your photo library. To save finished photographs. This is add-only access: the app can put photographs into your library and cannot read what is already there. That is also why it keeps its own copy. A gallery built on your library would have to ask for the whole library in order to show you a corner of it.
Importing. The Import button uses Apple's system photo picker, which runs outside the app. FRMT receives only the files you choose and never gains access to the rest.

### What is sent off the device
Nothing.
Photographs are developed on your iPhone's GPU. There is no cloud processing, no telemetry, no crash reporting service and no third-party code of any kind linked into the app.
If you use the share button on a photograph, iOS sends it wherever you choose. That is your action and your destination, and it is governed by whatever you shared it to.

### Children
FRMT is rated 4+ and collects no data from anyone, of any age.

### Changes
If this policy ever changes, the date at the top changes with it. Since the app collects nothing, any change would be a clarification rather than a new use of your data.

### Contact
Questions about this policy or the app: https://lf.wtf/frmt

# Privacy Policy — MODUL8
Source: https://lf.wtf/modul8/privacy/

MODUL8

## Privacy Policy
Last updated 22 November 2025
The short version. Your photos and videos are processed on your iPhone and are never uploaded anywhere. There is no account and no image server.
The free version shows ads through Google AdMob, and that is the one part of the app that involves a third party. Premium removes ads.

### What the app does with your media
MODUL8 needs access to your photo library for two things: loading the images or videos you choose, and saving the finished versions back. That is the whole of it.
All image and video processing happens locally on your device. Your originals and your edits are never uploaded to our servers or to any third-party server, and we have no access to the contents of your library.

### Usage data
Some usage data is collected automatically when you use the app. It may include your device type, mobile operating system, IP address, unique device identifiers and other diagnostic data, along with information about how and when the app is used.

### Advertising
We use Google AdMob to show ads in the free version. AdMob may collect and use:
- Device identifiers — the Advertising Identifier (IDFA) on iOS, only if you allow it at the App Tracking Transparency prompt.
- Usage data — information about how you interact with the ads.
This is used to serve personalised ads and to measure how they perform. You can turn personalised tracking off at any time in Settings › Privacy & Security › Tracking. For details on what Google collects, see the Google Privacy Policy.

### How the data is used
- To provide and maintain the app, including monitoring how it is used.
- To respond to requests you send us.
- To show advertisements through Google AdMob, which is what funds the free version.
- In the event of a merger, sale or other transfer of assets, information may be part of what transfers.

### Retention
Personal data is retained only as long as it is needed for the purposes described here, or as long as required to meet legal obligations, resolve disputes and enforce our agreements.

### Disclosure
We may have to disclose personal data if required to by law or in response to a valid request from a public authority such as a court or government agency. We may also disclose it in good faith where it is necessary to comply with a legal obligation, protect our rights or property, investigate possible wrongdoing connected to the app, protect the personal safety of users or the public, or defend against legal liability.

### Children
MODUL8 is not directed at anyone under 13, and we do not knowingly collect personally identifiable information from anyone under 13. If you are a parent or guardian and believe your child has given us personal data, please get in touch and we will remove it.

### Links to other sites
The app may link to sites we do not operate. We have no control over their content or their privacy practices, and we would suggest reading the policy of any site you visit.

### Changes to this policy
This policy may be updated from time to time. Any changes are posted on this page and take effect once posted, and the date at the top changes with them.

### Contact
Questions about this policy or about the app: L@LF.WTF

# Privacy — CYANO
Source: https://lf.wtf/cyano/privacy/

## Privacy Policy

Last updated: 16 August 2026

### The short version

CYANO does not collect anything about you, and it has no way to. There is no account, no analytics, no advertising and no server. The app contains no networking code of its own.

### What the app stores, and where

Everything stays on your iPhone.

Photographs. You choose a photograph from your library and the app turns it into a cyanotype. That happens entirely on the device, using its graphics hardware. The picture you chose is read, not copied: nothing is uploaded, and nothing is kept after you close the app. When you save or share a finished print, it goes to your photo library or to whichever app you picked in the share sheet, and that is the only copy that persists.

Settings. Whether you have seen the introduction, how many prints you have saved, which version last asked you for a rating, and whether the in-app purchase has been unlocked. These live in the app's own preferences and are read by nothing else.

### Permissions the app asks for

Photo library, to add. So a finished print can be saved. The app asks only for permission to add, not to read your whole library.

Choosing a photograph does not need a permission at all. The picker is run by iOS, and the app receives only the single picture you select. It never sees the rest of your library.

### The in-app purchase

CYANO is free, and one optional purchase unlocks the toning baths, the remaining papers and the second sensitiser formula. That purchase is handled entirely by Apple through the App Store. The app asks the system whether the purchase has been made and receives yes or no. It never sees your Apple Account, your name or any payment detail, and no payment information is stored in the app or sent anywhere by it.

Apple's own handling of that transaction is covered by Apple's privacy policy, not this one.

### What is not here

No analytics. No crash reporting. No advertising identifier. No third-party SDKs of any kind. No tracking across apps or websites. No mailing list. No cookies, because there is no website inside the app.

Because none of this exists, there is also nothing to opt out of and no data to request or delete. Deleting the app removes its preferences with it.

### Children

CYANO is rated 4+ and is safe for any age. It collects nothing from anybody, children included.

### Changes

If this policy ever changes, the date at the top of this page changes with it. Since the app collects nothing, any change would be a matter of wording rather than of practice.

### Contact

Questions about this policy: https://lf.wtf/cyano
